newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr depressed on US$, buoyed by yen.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr depressed on US$, buoyed by yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar eked out a modest bounce Friday to end a four-day run of lower closes, but was still 1/2 cent off on the week and short of key levels.

Traders said the currency edged up from Thursday's US$0.7701 low after corporate and Asian support proved unexpectedly solid and enjoyed a further short squeeze when both the yen and mark came under renewed pressure this afternoon.

But fresh offshore offers stopped the rally short of resistance at US$0.7750, so keeping the chart outlook bearish, while uncertainty over domestic interest rates ensured offshore investors preferred the U.S. dollar to the local variety.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local currency had fetched up at US$0.7731/36 after struggling higher from an early US$0.7717/22 and US$0.7710/15 late here Thursday.
The latter level had been the dollar's lowest local close since March last year and a big come down from the six-year high of US$0.8212 hit less than two months ago.

In the process it had breached a book full of chart levels and built up a bearish momentum that would be hard to shake loose. Thus while the 74 cent level was expected to provide some psychological support, analysts reckoned the impetus was there to test the August intra-day low of US$0.7680 next week.
If that were to fail then a full fledged downtrend to 75 cents or lower would be on the cards.
The story was radically different on the crosses, however, as the yen and mark had enough troubles of their own that the local dollar looked a haven of tranquility.

The yen took a late hit when the Bank of Japan said yen weakness was haing no major negative impact on the economy. The market took that as a sign the BOJ would not intervene to support the currency and the dollar jumped to 92.73/83 yen from 91.93/03 late here Thursday. In this it was following the U.S. dollar which shot to 120.00 yen from an early 119.05/10.

The yen, and most European currencies for that matter, had been on the slide since it became clear the fragile state of the economic recoveries in Japan and Germany meant interest rates would remain stuck at record lows for months to come.

This outlook had proved more beneficial to the U.S. dollar than the local currency since the strength of the U.S. economy meant the next move in rates there was likely to be upwards while the risk in Australia was for another policy easing.
Some of the heat had gone out of the speculation following the revelation that jobs growth had been underestimated since August, but analysts still saw an evens chance of a cut in Q1.
The chance of another easing may become clearer next week when consumer price data for the December quarter are released.

These are expected to show underlying inflation slowed to 2.1 percent from 2.4 percent in Q3 and a high of 3.3 a year ago. That would be the very bottom of the Reserve Bank's 2-3 percent target band and would provide the scope for a cut if the bank felt one was needed as insurance.
The RBA policy making board meets to decide on rates on February 4 and the dollar was likely to remain under pressure until then.
